particulars: All names, dates, places, ages, heights and weights, statistics, sentence lengths and compensation amounts were dropped (Houston 1998 abduction and rape, two teenagers, 1 in 694,000 vs 1 in 8, 25 years, $118,000 plus annuity, the CODIS hit in 2006).

items.record: The case starts with a crime victim's eyewitness identification at a show-up: "From a distance of about 10 feet, she told police she was positive", even though the suspect did not match her own description.
items.reading: absent; the reading frames the case as an institution acting on inflated internal metrics or vendor assurances.
items.loss: The originating event and the role of a mistaken eyewitness as an independent source of the false account are missing.

items.record: The harmed party is a single teenage criminal defendant who was wrongfully convicted and imprisoned: "convicted on July 9, 1999, and sentenced to 25 years in prison."
items.reading: Scattered isolates such as contractors, franchisees, claimants or frontline staff, many people each facing the institution alone.
items.loss: The reading gets wrong who was harmed, how many, and what was at stake (liberty, not money or contracts).

items.record: The flawed account was forensic science: an outdated, low-discrimination DNA method, analyst errors and overstated statistics, "1 in 694,000" against an actual "better than 1 chance in 8."
items.reading: Inflated performance metrics or self-assessments reported up a chain of command by units seeking to look good.
items.loss: The reading misidentifies the mechanism of inflation: technical misstatement of match probability, not incentive-driven reporting.

items.record: The lab's internal inconsistencies went unnoticed: it "obtained different profiles when typing samples from the same person," and its report wrongly said a sample implicated him when "he had been excluded."
items.loss: Concrete internal errors that should have exposed the flaw are not recovered.

items.record: Exculpatory evidence was actively cut off at trial: "I don't want to talk about the unknown sample, okay?"
items.reading: Suppression is described as procedural dismissal of complaints, not as an adversary blocking evidence in open court.
items.loss: A specific suppressive act by the prosecution at trial is missing.

items.record: Defense counsel failed him: he told his client "that's what they came up with," never authorized the paid independent test, retained no expert, and opened the door to prior-conduct questions.
items.loss: The failure of the defendant's own advocate, a key link in the harm, is not recovered.

items.record: The appeal was rejected on the strength of the flawed evidence itself: "The State's DNA evidence ... is not seriously challenged."
items.reading: Partly recovered as general institutional rationalizing, but not as a court relying on the same flawed record.
items.loss: The way the error was locked in through appellate review is missing.

items.record: The break came through a sequence: defense lawyers tipped reporters, independent experts reviewed records, the broadcast aired, the mother saw it and called the station, then the expert review, retesting and release followed.
items.reading: A predicted generic outside rupture via press or courts, with "the record still stands" at the moment captured.
items.loss: The actual chain of exposure, including family agency and the defendant's own self-drafted motion, is missing, and the reading wrongly places the case before resolution.

items.record: Prosecutors resisted after exoneration: they "declined to support a pardon based on innocence, noting that the victim had not recanted," and opposed the habeas petition even after repeated exclusions.
items.loss: The institution's continued resistance after the error was proven is missing.

items.record: Full resolution: a pardon based on innocence, state compensation, and a database hit identifying the real perpetrator, who "pleaded guilty" and named an accomplice.
items.reading: Lists the outcome as unknown and says redress may never have come.
items.loss: The ending, including formal vindication, redress and identification of the true offenders, is not recovered.

items.record: The wider context was a systemic crime lab scandal that this case exemplified: reporters were "investigating the Houston crime lab after receiving a tip ... about problems with the lab's work."
items.reading: Proposes many cases multiplying, but frames them as isolated complainants rather than a broad audit of one lab.
items.loss: The relation between one wrongful conviction and a broader failure of a forensic institution is only vaguely recovered.
